section_summary: This section covers diplomatic, political, and intelligence reports from August to October 1942 concerning Japanese domestic and foreign policy during World War II. It begins with documentation and press reports on ultranationalist Shinto wartime ideology and the divine mission doctrines of Chikao Fujisawa, alongside intelligence representations submitted by Kilsoo K. Haan of the Sino-Korean Peoples' League regarding Japanese-German friction over a prospective Siberian campaign. Later records examine the political crisis culminating in the resignation of Foreign Minister Shigenori Togo, the contentious establishment of the Ministry of Greater East Asia under Prime Minister Hideki Tojo, eyewitness impressions of Japanese wartime society from returned Chilean journalist Augusto Iglesias, and Allied diplomatic evaluations of Japanese civilian morale and military movements.

subfiles.about: Typed transcript of the concluding pages of Chikao Fujisawa's Shinto ideological pamphlet 'Divine Mission of Nippon,' collected by E. W. Koons aboard the M.S. Gripsholm.
subfiles.summary: This subfile contains a typed transcript of the concluding pages (pages 34-40) of Professor Chikao Fujisawa's booklet 'Divine Mission of Nippon,' exploring Shinto theological justifications for Japan's holy war and the concept of Hakko Ichiu. The text discusses the O-harai purification prayer, Misogi, and quotes biblical scriptures from Acts and Revelation to argue that all nations originated from the divine imperial center embodied by the Japanese Emperor. An appended explanatory note by American detainee E. W. Koons, written aboard the exchange ship M.S. Gripsholm on August 2, 1942, records that the pamphlet was obtained from a Korean police liaison detective at the West Gate Police Station detention camp in Keijo.
subfiles.title: Excerpt from 'Divine Mission of Nippon' by Chikao Fujisawa, with Note by E. W. Koons

subfiles.about: A cabled press dispatch from Stockholm reporting on the ultranationalist Shinto booklet 'Divine Mission of Nippon' by Professor Chikao Fujisawa.
subfiles.from: New York Times correspondent in Stockholm
subfiles.summary: A press cable sent from Stockholm describes a booklet published in Tokyo in February 1942 by Professor Chikao Fujisawa, characterizing it as Japan's ideological equivalent to Hitler's Mein Kampf. The dispatch outlines Fujisawa's depiction of Japan as the sacred cradle of human civilization and the Emperor as the cosmic life-center destined to unite humanity into a single patriarchal family under Hakko Ichiu. The report notes Fujisawa's attacks on Anglo-American capitalistic individualism and Soviet communism, highlights philosophical affinities between the Axis powers, and critiques Fujisawa's pseudo-scientific racial claims.
subfiles.title: Stockholm Press Dispatch on Chikao Fujisawa's 'Divine Mission of Nippon'

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note regarding Japanese publications transmitted to Philippine President Manuel L. Quezon via British Consul General Wyatt-Smith.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet records a communication dated August 27, 1942, from American Foreign Service Officer James B. Butrick (formerly at Peiping, currently in the United States). The paper concerns Japanese publications forwarded to President Manuel L. Quezon of the Commonwealth of the Philippines at the request of British Consul General Wyatt-Smith in Manila. The underlying document is cross-referenced to file number 740.0011 Pacific War/2772.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Japanese Publications for Transmission to President Quezon

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram reporting Tokyo intelligence from French Ambassador Charles Arsène-Henry concerning the resignation of Japanese Foreign Minister Shigenori Togo.
subfiles.summary: American Chargé d'Affaires S. Pinkney Tuck in Vichy transmits intelligence from two telegrams sent by French Ambassador Charles Arsène-Henry in Tokyo regarding the sudden resignation of Foreign Minister Shigenori Togo. The telegram details that Togo and other diplomats resigned primarily in protest against Premier Hideki Tojo's creation of a new Ministry of Greater East Asia, which strips the Foreign Office of jurisdiction over Asian affairs. Secondary factors cited include disagreements over neutrality with Soviet Russia and friction between civilian diplomats and the military. General Tojo's efforts to find a successor among career diplomats such as Hachiro Arita, Masayuki Tani, and Saburo Kurusu are also reported.
subfiles.title: Vichy Telegram No. 1303 on Resignation of Foreign Minister Togo and Proposed Ministry of Greater East Asia

subfiles.about: Telegram from Chungking reporting Chinese military intelligence claims of an imperial Privy Council meeting portending imminent Japanese military action against Russia.
subfiles.summary: American Ambassador Clarence E. Gauss transmits a report received by the U.S. Military Attaché from the Chinese Chief of Military Intelligence stating that Emperor Hirohito presided over a meeting of the Japanese Privy Council on September 16, 1942. The Chinese intelligence chief interpreted the meeting as signaling imminent drastic action, specifically a possible Japanese attack on the Soviet Union. Gauss cautions that the Embassy has received no corroborating information from other sources to verify the report or its source. Department paraphrase copies prepared on September 17 and 18, 1942, accompany the incoming cable.
subfiles.title: Chungking Telegram No. 1057 and Paraphrases on Japanese Privy Council Meeting

subfiles.about: Letter with supporting documents from Kilsoo K. Haan of the Sino-Korean Peoples' League analyzing Japan's cabinet crisis, German pressure to invade Siberia, and Pacific strategy.
subfiles.summary: Kilsoo K. Haan, Washington Representative of the Sino-Korean Peoples' League and Korean National Front Federation, submits an intelligence analysis to President Franklin D. Roosevelt regarding a Cabinet crisis in Tokyo. Haan asserts that German Ambassador Eugen Ott and the Kwantung Army urged Premier Hideki Tojo to invade Siberia following the German advance on Stalingrad, but Tojo rejected the demand due to adverse winter weather and instead prioritized southern operations toward Port Moresby, Australia, and India. The letter includes enclosures showcasing public endorsements of Haan's past intelligence work, an eleven-point political manifesto adopted by the Korean National Revolutionary Congress in November 1941, and news clippings detailing Haan's warnings prior to Pearl Harbor.
subfiles.title: Letter from Kilsoo K. Haan to President Roosevelt with Enclosures on Japanese War Plans and Siberian Policy

subfiles.about: State Department acknowledgement informing Kilsoo K. Haan that his communication to President Roosevelt was received and shared with military departments.
subfiles.summary: George Atcheson, Jr., Assistant Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, acknowledges receipt of Kilsoo K. Haan's letter of September 3, 1942, addressed to President Roosevelt concerning the resignation of Japanese Foreign Minister Shigenori Togo. Atcheson informs Haan that his views have been carefully noted. He further states that because the letter and enclosures touch upon military matters, copies have been forwarded to the War and Navy Departments for their information.
subfiles.title: State Department Acknowledgement to Kilsoo K. Haan

subfiles.about: Official transmittal forwarding a copy of Kilsoo K. Haan's letter and accompanying maps to Secretary of War Henry L. Stimson.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits to Secretary of War Henry L. Stimson a copy of the September 3, 1942, letter sent to President Roosevelt by Kilsoo K. Haan regarding the resignation of the Japanese Foreign Minister. The communication notes that two maps received under cover of Haan's letter are also enclosed for the War Department's potential interest.
subfiles.title: State Department Transmittal to the Secretary of War regarding Kilsoo K. Haan Letter

subfiles.about: Official transmittal forwarding a copy of Kilsoo K. Haan's letter and accompanying maps to Secretary of the Navy Frank Knox.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits to Secretary of the Navy Frank Knox a copy of Kilsoo K. Haan's letter of September 3, 1942, to President Roosevelt regarding the causes behind the resignation of the Japanese Foreign Minister. Copies of two maps enclosed with Haan's original communication are also transmitted for the Navy Department's consideration.
subfiles.title: State Department Transmittal to the Secretary of the Navy regarding Kilsoo K. Haan Letter

subfiles.about: Internal memorandum summarizing Despatch No. 4434 from Santiago on Chilean journalist Augusto Iglesias's observations in Japan.
subfiles.summary: An internal memorandum prepared within the Division of Far Eastern Affairs summarizes Despatch No. 4434 from Ambassador Claude G. Bowers in Santiago regarding an interview with Chilean journalist Augusto Iglesias following his return from Japan. The memo highlights that although Iglesias was previously pro-German, his visit convinced him that only an American victory could safeguard the Pacific nations, due to visceral Japanese anti-white sentiments and intense martial discipline. It also notes Iglesias's conclusions that Japan secretly fears Soviet forces in Siberia and will not attack Russia, hoping instead for a negotiated peace between Germany and the USSR.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Summary of Interview with Chilean Journalist Augusto Iglesias

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch forwarding a detailed Embassy memorandum of a confidential interview with returned Chilean journalist Augusto Iglesias.
subfiles.summary: American Ambassador Claude G. Bowers at Santiago transmits a confidential report prepared by Biddle H. Garrison of the Embassy Press Section based on an extensive interview with Chilean writer Augusto Iglesias, who visited Japan under German sponsorship. Iglesias describes the pervasive police surveillance, austere standard rations, Emperor worship, and the severe psychological shock delivered by the Doolittle air raid on Tokyo. He emphasizes pervasive Japanese hostility toward all white nationalities—including German and Italian Axis partners—as well as Japanese respect and fear of Soviet military strength following border clashes, leading Iglesias to conclude that Japan will avoid war with Russia and that only an American victory can preserve Pacific security.
subfiles.title: Santiago Despatch No. 4434 Enclosing Memorandum of Interview with Augusto Iglesias on Wartime Japan

subfiles.about: Departmental memorandum summarizing an analysis by Chinese diplomat Yang Yun-chu on the establishment of the Greater East Asia Ministry and Togo's resignation.
subfiles.summary: Robert L. Smyth of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs reviews Despatch No. 636 from Chungking, which enclosed an article by Yang Yun-chu, former Chinese Chargé d'Affaires in Tokyo. The memorandum outlines Yang's view that Togo's resignation marked the decisive victory of Japanese militarists over professional Foreign Office diplomats and moderates. It explains that Togo had initially been appointed to pacify the Soviet Union and project a moderate image to the West, but became superfluous after the Pacific War began and was forced out when he opposed the creation of the Greater East Asia Affairs Ministry, followed by the resignations of Vice-Minister Nishi and Ambassador Kawagoe.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Summary of Despatch No. 636 on Resignation of Foreign Minister Togo

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting an English translation of a Central Daily News article by Yang Yun-chu analyzing Japanese militarist ascendancy over the Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: American Ambassador Clarence E. Gauss in Chungking forwards a translated article from the Central Daily News by Yang Yun-chu, Director of the East Asiatic Affairs Department of the Chinese Foreign Ministry. Yang analyzes the creation of the Greater East Asia Ministry and the resignation of Foreign Minister Shigenori Togo as the culmination of long-standing clashes between the Japanese military and career diplomats dating back to General Ugaki's resignation in 1937 and the 1939 trade ministry dispute under Nomura. Yang argues that Tojo's concentration of power represents an open military dictatorship preparing for a protracted war, and cautions occupied territories in Southeast Asia against trusting Japanese rule.
subfiles.title: Chungking Despatch No. 636 Enclosing Article by Yang Yun-chu on the Greater East Asia Ministry

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram reporting Tokyo Embassy intelligence regarding Kazuo Aoki's appointment to the Greater East Asia Ministry and declining Japanese civilian morale.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires S. Pinkney Tuck in Vichy transmits intelligence from a French Embassy cable sent from Tokyo on October 19, 1942. The report discloses that Kazuo Aoki has been selected to head the new Ministry of Greater Asia after the military's effort to appoint General Terauchi failed, reflecting a priority to settle the war in China. Additionally, the French Ambassador reports growing moral uncertainty and anxiety among the Japanese populace caused by repatriates returning from the United States who described American industrial war output, prompting an official domestic press campaign warning against American air raids and feeding public rumors of troop movements toward Siberia.
subfiles.title: Vichy Telegram No. 1567 on Appointment of Aoki, Civilian Morale, and Siberian Rumors

subfiles.about: Confidential telegram instructing the Chungking Embassy on sharing intelligence concerning Kazuo Aoki, Japanese public morale, and troop movements in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State instructs the American Embassy in Chungking regarding recent Tokyo intelligence obtained from French diplomatic sources. The cable confirms that Kazuo Aoki has been slated to lead the Ministry of Greater East Asia over General Terauchi and notes widespread civilian anxiety triggered by repatriates returning from America with reports of massive U.S. war production. Ambassador Gauss is authorized, at his discretion and without revealing the source, to share information regarding Aoki's appointment, public morale anxieties, and Manchurian troop movements with the Chinese government.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram No. 1004 to Chungking on Tokyo Political and Morale Developments

subfiles.about: Internal memorandum discussing the distribution of intelligence from Vichy Telegram No. 1567 to the British and Chinese governments.
subfiles.summary: Robert L. Smyth of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs responds to a memorandum from Political Adviser Stanley K. Hornbeck concerning Vichy Telegram No. 1567. Smyth reports that Theodore C. Achilles of the Division of European Affairs had already orally communicated the substance of the Vichy cable to the British Embassy. Smyth attaches a revised draft telegram authorizing the American Embassy in Chungking to communicate selected portions of the intelligence to Chinese authorities, noting that European Division officers Hugh S. Cumming, Jr. and J. Wesley Jones concur.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Sharing Vichy Intelligence with British and Chinese

subfiles.about: Memorandum by Stanley K. Hornbeck advising that Tokyo intelligence from Vichy would be more valuable to the British than to the Chinese.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations, provides his opinion on the handling of the Tokyo intelligence transmitted in Vichy Telegram No. 1567. Hornbeck suggests that the information would likely be of greater value to the British Government than to the Chinese Government. He advises that whether the report is dispatched to London, Chungking, or both, the outgoing instruction should direct the receiving mission to communicate at least part of the substance to the host government.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Adviser on Political Relations Hornbeck regarding Dissemination of Tokyo Intelligence
